title: Comparison: diff, cmp, comm, patch
lead: Compare two files, two directories and two lists, read the difference, create and apply patches, and use exit codes in scripts.
objectives: You read `diff` output (normal and `-u` unified), including `@@` hunks and `+`/`-` lines.
You compare directories and files quickly with `diff -r`, `diff -q`, `cmp` and `sha256sum -c`.
You find differences between sorted lists with `comm`, and common or unique lines with `sort | uniq -d/-u`.
You create patches with `diff -u`, apply them with `patch`, undo them with `-R`, and check exit codes (0/1/2).

sections.title: diff: line-by-line differences
body: `diff old new` compares two text files line by line and prints the changes needed to turn the old file into the new one. In normal output you see a command line such as `2c2` (line 2 changed); `<` marks lines from the first file, `>` lines from the second.

In practice the **unified** format (`-u`) is the standard: `---` is the first file, `+++` the second; the hunk `@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@` means three lines starting at line 1 in the first file and four lines starting at line 1 in the second. Lines starting with `-` exist only in the old file, lines with `+` only in the new one; lines starting with a space are context. Git and patch tools use this format.

**Exit code:** `0` files identical, `1` differences found, `2` trouble (file missing, unreadable). So `diff` reports 'failure' when it finds differences; that is not an error. In the simulator `diff`, `cmp`, `comm` and `patch` do not run; try them on your own VM. Here the simulator only checks that you typed the command, plus the prepared files.

commands.what: Shows the difference between two files in normal format (with `<` and `>` lines).
commands.where: When comparing two versions of a configuration file.
commands.why: You see what changed without reading the whole file.

commands.what: Unified format: `---`/`+++` header, `@@` hunks and `+`/`-` lines.
commands.where: When sharing changes, in code review, when creating patches.
commands.why: Context lines make clear where the change is.

commands.what: Prints only 'Files ... differ', or nothing.
commands.where: When only 'same or not' matters; in scripts.
commands.why: No long output, the exit code is still 0/1.

commands.what: Shows two columns side by side; differences marked with `|`, `<`, `>`.
commands.where: When comparing short files by eye.
commands.why: You see both versions next to each other.

commands.what: Ignores whitespace differences (indentation, trailing spaces).
commands.where: For files that were only reformatted.
commands.why: Noise disappears, real content differences remain.

sections.tip: Which file is 'old' and which is 'new'? Order matters: `diff old new`. Swap them and `+` and `-` swap too.
sections.warn: Files created on Windows carry `\r` (CRLF) at each line end, so every line looks different. Clean up with `tr -d '\r' < win.txt > fixed.txt` or use `diff --strip-trailing-cr`.

sections.title: Comparing directories
body: `diff -r dir_a dir_b` compares two directory trees recursively. For files that exist in only one directory it prints `Only in dir_a: extra.txt`; for files with different content it prints the diff. With `-q` (or `-rq`) you see only which files differ; ideal for checking a backup with many files.

You can also compare the output of two commands: `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)` (process substitution, a **bash** feature) hands the outputs over like temporary files. It does not work in plain `sh`.

commands.what: Compares two directories including subdirectories.
commands.where: When comparing two project versions or a backup.
commands.why: Missing, extra and changed files in one go.

commands.what: Lists only files that differ or exist on one side only.
commands.where: For backup verification, in large trees.
commands.why: A short overview; look at single files in detail afterwards.

commands.what: Compares the output of two commands like files (bash).
commands.where: For sorted lists or comparing two environments.
commands.why: No intermediate files needed.

sections.tip: Direction does not matter, but for readability always write the 'reference' directory first.

sections.title: cmp and checksums
body: `cmp` compares files **byte by byte** and reports the byte and line number of the first difference. For binary files `diff` only says 'Binary files differ'; `cmp` shows the exact position. `cmp -s` prints nothing, only the exit code (0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble). In scripts: `if cmp -s a b; then echo same; fi`.

If the files are on different machines you cannot compare them directly; compute a **checksum**. `sha256sum notes.txt` produces a hash; identical content gives an identical hash. `sha256sum -c sums.txt` recomputes stored hashes and prints `OK` or `FAILED`. This is how you verify a download is intact. `md5sum` is outdated; use `sha256sum` for security.

commands.what: Compares two files byte by byte and reports the position of the first difference.
commands.where: For binary files and to verify copies.
commands.why: Gives a definite answer even for non-text files.

commands.what: Silent comparison; the result is only in the exit code.
commands.where: In scripts as an `if` condition.
commands.why: Decides 'same?' without output.

commands.what: Computes the SHA-256 hash of a file.
commands.where: For verifying downloads and backups.
commands.why: You compare contents without having the files side by side.

commands.what: Checks a hash list; prints `OK` or `FAILED` per file.
commands.where: For ISO images or backups.
commands.why: Shows automatically whether anything is corrupted or changed.

sections.tip: See the exit code with `echo $?` right after the command; if another command runs in between, the value is gone.

sections.title: Comparing lists: comm, uniq
body: `comm a b` shows two **sorted** files in three columns: column 1 only in a, column 2 only in b, column 3 in both. `-1`, `-2`, `-3` hide that column: `comm -12` = common lines, `comm -23` = only in a, `comm -13` = only in b.
**Pitfall:** if the input is not sorted, `comm` gives wrong results and warns 'file 2 is not in sorted order'. Sort first: `sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt`.

Without `comm`, `sort a b | uniq -d` gives lines present in both lists (duplicated ones) and `sort a b | uniq -u` gives lines that appear only once. Each list should be free of duplicates itself, otherwise the counting breaks. Both commands also work in the simulator.

commands.what: Compares two sorted files in three columns.
commands.where: When comparing user, package or IP lists.
commands.why: Separates common and unique lines in one command.

commands.what: Shows only lines present in both files.
commands.where: When you need the intersection.
commands.why: Hides columns 1 and 2, the common one remains.

commands.what: Shows only lines present in the first file.
commands.where: For the question 'I have it, you don't'.
commands.why: Finds missing or surplus entries.

commands.what: From merged sorted lines, prints the duplicated (common) ones.
commands.where: Without `comm`, or for a quick intersection.
commands.why: Works everywhere with standard tools.

commands.what: Prints only lines that occur exactly once (symmetric difference).
commands.where: When looking for lines that are in only one of the lists.
commands.why: Eliminates the common lines.

sections.tip: Rule of thumb: always `sort` before `comm`; and use the same locale (`LC_ALL=C`) afterwards, otherwise the sort order may not match.

sections.title: Create and apply patches: patch
body: `diff -u old new > change.patch` writes the difference to a file. Someone else applies it with `patch` to their old copy: `patch work.txt < change.patch`. For directory trees you create `diff -ruN old/ new/ > all.patch`; when applying, `-p1` strips the first path component (`old/`), `-p0` uses paths unchanged.
Before applying, try `patch --dry-run < change.patch`: it changes nothing and tells you whether the hunks fit. On failures a `.rej` file is created. `patch -R < change.patch` undoes the patch.
A patch relies on context lines; if the file was changed elsewhere in the meantime, applying can fail or shift (`fuzz`).

commands.what: Writes the difference in unified format to a patch file.
commands.where: To hand a change to someone else.
commands.why: Only the changed lines are transported, not the whole file.

commands.what: Applies the changes in a patch file to a file.
commands.where: When working a received patch into your copy.
commands.why: Applies only the difference instead of replacing the whole file.

commands.what: Tests the patch without actually applying it.
commands.where: Before patching important files.
commands.why: You spot mismatches without changing anything.

commands.what: Reverses the patch (undoes it).
commands.where: When an applied patch causes problems.
commands.why: Restores the state before the patch.

sections.tip: If the patch is for a directory tree, run it from the project root and try `--dry-run` first.
sections.warn: `patch` modifies files in place. For important files make a backup first with `cp work.txt work.txt.orig`, and on your VM take a snapshot first.
sections.danger: Do not apply patches to the root directory (`/`) or system configuration; work only in your practice folder. A wrong `-p` value changes the wrong files.

t01.hint: The simulator has no diff; typing the command is enough. You will see the real output on your VM.

t02.text: Compare the same files in unified format: `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt`.
t02.hint: `-u` means unified; the output contains `@@` hunks.

t03.text: Compare byte by byte with `cmp v1.txt v2.txt`.
t03.hint: cmp reports the byte and line number of the first difference.

t04.text: Copy `v1.txt` with `cp v1.txt v1.bak` and verify they are identical with `diff -q v1.txt v1.bak`.
t04.hint: If identical, `diff -q` prints nothing and the exit code is 0.

t05.text: Compare the directories `dir_a` and `dir_b` with `diff -rq dir_a dir_b`.
t05.hint: `-r` recursive, `-q` short summary. `-r dir_a dir_b` is accepted too.

t06.text: `list_b.txt` is not sorted. For `comm`, create a sorted copy with `sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt`.
t06.hint: The redirect `>` writes the sorted output into a new file.

t07.text: Use `comm -12 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt` to show the lines present in both lists.
t07.hint: `-12` hides columns 1 and 2; the common column remains.

t08.text: Predict, then run: `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -d`. Which names appear?
t08.hint: `uniq -d` prints only lines that occur more than once.

t09.text: Predict, then run: `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u`. Which names appear?
t09.hint: `-u` prints only lines that occur once: names that are in only one of the two lists.

t10.text: Predict: what does `grep -q debug v1.txt ; echo $?` print? Run it to check.
t10.hint: `grep -q` returns 0 if found, 1 if not; `v1.txt` contains no debug.

t11.text: Debug: `win.txt` looks different on every line because it has Windows line endings (`\r`). Create a clean copy with `tr -d '\r' < win.txt > fixed.txt`.
t11.hint: `tr -d` deletes the given character; redirect input with `<`, output with `>`.

t12.text: Mini project: copy with `cp v1.txt work.txt`, create a patch with `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > change.patch`, then apply it with `patch work.txt < change.patch`.
t12.hint: Three commands in order; diff and patch do not run in the simulator, try them on your VM.

t13.text: Challenge: write only the names that are in `list_a.txt` (not in `list_b.txt`) to the file `only_a.txt`. Without `comm`; hint: pass `list_b.txt` twice.
t13.hint: `sort list_a.txt list_b.txt list_b.txt | uniq -u > only_a.txt`: names from b occur at least twice, names only in a occur once.

t14.text: Copy with `cp v1.txt same.txt`, run `cmp -s v1.txt same.txt` and type `echo $?` right after.
t14.hint: In one line this also works: `cmp -s v1.txt same.txt ; echo $?`.

t15.text: Predict, then run: `cut -d= -f1 v1.txt`. Which keys are listed?
t15.hint: `-d=` is the delimiter, `-f1` the first field: everything before the `=`.

t16.text: TICKET #3701 — Change review: back up `v2.txt` as `v2.bak`, save the difference to `v1.txt` with `diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > review.patch`, and write `review done` into `report.txt`.
t16.hint: Three steps: `cp`, `diff -u ... > review.patch`, `echo review done > report.txt`.

q1.q: With which exit code does `diff a b` end when the files differ?
q1.explain: 0 identical, 1 differences, 2 trouble. A difference is not an error, but it is not zero either.

q2.q: What does `comm` need from its input files to work correctly?
q2.explain: comm expects sorted input; otherwise the result is wrong. Apply `sort` first.

q3.q: What does a line starting with `+` mean in unified diff output?
options: The line existed only in the old file
The line is only in the new file (added)
q3.explain: `-` was removed from the old file, `+` added to the new one; lines starting with a space are context.

q4.q: Which command undoes an applied patch?
q4.explain: `patch -R` reverses the patch; the patch file is read from standard input.

summary: `diff -u old new` shows the change; exit code 0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble.
`diff -rq` checks directories, `cmp` compares bytes, `sha256sum -c` verifies content integrity.
`comm` works only on sorted input; alternatives: `sort | uniq -d` (common) and `uniq -u` (unique).
Create a patch with `diff -u > change.patch`, test with `patch --dry-run`, apply with `patch`, undo with `patch -R`.
Pitfalls: unsorted `comm`, CRLF line endings, `diff` on binary files.

glossary.meaning: A change block in unified diff that starts with `@@` and includes context lines.
A file holding diff output; the `patch` command applies it to files.
A command's final status, read with `$?`. For diff: 0 same, 1 different, 2 trouble.
A hash value computed from content; if the content changes, the value changes.
Windows line ending (`\r\n`); Linux uses only `\n`.

vm.intro: Run the following commands on your own VM in the `~/lab` folder. They only create files in this practice folder and do not touch system settings.

v01.title: diff: normal and unified
v01.text: Create two small files and see the difference in both formats. Paste the unified output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab
printf 'port=80
host=linux-lab
mode=prod
' > v1.txt
printf 'port=8080
host=linux-lab
mode=prod
debug=on
' > v2.txt
diff v1.txt v2.txt
diff -u v1.txt v2.txt

differs: Date and time will differ; what matters are the `@@`, `-` and `+` lines.
If there is no output, the files are identical; re-check the `printf` lines.

v02.title: Exit codes
v02.text: See `diff -q`, `cmp -s` and the exit codes. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
diff -q v1.txt v2.txt; echo "exit=$?"
cp v1.txt same.txt
cmp -s v1.txt same.txt; echo "exit=$?"
diff v1.txt missing.txt; echo "exit=$?"
blocks.expected:
Files v1.txt and v2.txt differ
exit=1
exit=0
diff: missing.txt: No such file or directory
exit=2

differs: If your system language differs, the message may be translated; the `exit=` values must match.
If you see `exit=0` on the first line, `v2.txt` was not created; run v01 again.

v03.title: comm and uniq
v03.text: Compare two name lists. First see the warning for unsorted `comm`, then the right way.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
printf 'alice\nbob\ncarol\ndave\n' > list_a.txt
printf 'erin\nbob\ncarol\n' > list_b.txt
comm -12 list_a.txt list_b.txt
sort list_b.txt > sorted_b.txt
comm -12 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt
comm -23 list_a.txt sorted_b.txt
sort list_a.txt list_b.txt | uniq -d
diff <(sort list_a.txt) <(sort list_b.txt)
blocks.expected:
comm: file 2 is not in sorted order
bob
carol
alice
dave
bob
carol
1d0
< alice
...

differs: With unsorted input the `comm` warning may not appear or the output may be incomplete; the result is undefined, so always `sort` first.
If `diff <(...)` gives a `syntax error`, your shell is not bash; type `bash` and try again.

v04.title: Create, test, apply and undo a patch
v04.text: Turn a copy of `v1.txt` into `v2.txt` with a patch and undo it. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
diff -u v1.txt v2.txt > change.patch
cp v1.txt work.txt
patch --dry-run work.txt < change.patch
patch work.txt < change.patch
cat work.txt
patch -R work.txt < change.patch
cat work.txt
blocks.expected:
checking file work.txt
patching file work.txt
port=8080
host=linux-lab
mode=prod
debug=on
patching file work.txt
port=80
host=linux-lab
mode=prod

differs: If you see `patch: command not found`: on Ubuntu `sudo apt install patch`, on Rocky/Alma `sudo dnf install patch`.
If `--dry-run` is not supported (very old version), skip that line.
If you see `Hunk #1 FAILED`, `work.txt` is not identical to `v1.txt`; start over with `cp v1.txt work.txt`.

v05.title: Checksums
v05.text: Compute hashes, then modify a file and catch the corruption with `sha256sum -c`. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
sha256sum v1.txt same.txt
sha256sum v1.txt > sums.txt
sha256sum -c sums.txt
echo 'x' >> v1.txt
sha256sum -c sums.txt
blocks.expected:
<64 hex characters>  v1.txt
<64 hex characters>  same.txt
v1.txt: OK
v1.txt: FAILED
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match

differs: The first two hashes must be identical (`v1.txt` and `same.txt` have the same content).
On a non-English system the warning text may be translated; `OK` and `FAILED` stay the same.
If `same.txt` is missing, run the step from v02.
